incidents.name: BIND 9 high-severity GSS-TSIG memory corruption flaw (CVE-2026-94300)
incidents.subject: BIND 9
incidents.summary: ISC disclosed CVE-2026-94300, a high-severity (CVSS 8.1) memory corruption bug in BIND 9's named. Replaying a captured GSS-TSIG signed UDP message while its key is valid can corrupt memory and may potentially lead to remote code execution. ISC knows of no active exploits and lists no workaround. Patched releases are available.
incidents.dateLabel: Publicly disclosed 21 Oct 2026 (early notice 14 Oct)

sources.label: ISC advisory: CVE-2026-94300, Concurrent GSS-TSIG messages corrupt memory
AJ Stuyvenberg (@astuyve) post amplifying the ISC advisory

incidents.correction: This is a vulnerability advisory, not a breach. ISC says it is not aware of active exploits. The flaw is rated Exploitable: Remotely, but ISC describes remote code execution as a potential outcome and the attack needs a captured GSS-TSIG signed UDP message replayed while its negotiated key is still valid, plus crafted queries to an attacker-controlled zone. Not every BIND or DNS deployment uses GSS-TSIG. The advisory was posted on 21 Oct, not 23 Oct.

detail.whatHappened: ISC's advisory says replaying GSS-TSIG signed UDP messages can corrupt memory in named, the BIND 9 server. An attacker who captured a previously signed message can replay it while the negotiated TSIG key is still valid. By also sending crafted queries to a zone the attacker controls, the attacker may potentially achieve remote code execution. ISC found the flaw in internal testing; Dave Aitel of OpenAI independently found and reported it. ISC gave early notice on 14 Oct and public disclosure on 21 Oct. A popular X post on 23 Oct brought wider attention.
detail.exposure: Affected: BIND 9.11.0 to 9.18.50, 9.20.0 to 9.20.29 and 9.21.0 to 9.21.26, plus Supported Preview Edition 9.11.3-S1 to 9.18.50-S1 and 9.20.9-S1 to 9.20.29-S1. ISC rates it High, CVSS 8.1 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H). Impact is program abort and potential remote code execution. High attack complexity reflects the replay and key-validity conditions.
detail.fix: Upgrade to the patched release closest to your version: 9.20.30 or 9.21.27, or 9.20.30-S1 for Supported Preview Edition. ISC lists no workarounds.
detail.remaining: ISC says it knows of no active exploits. The advisory does not give a count of exposed servers or say how many deployments use GSS-TSIG. It also does not name a patched release for the older 9.11 to 9.18 branches, so operators on those branches should check ISC's security matrix.

responses.summary: Published the advisory with fixed versions 9.20.30, 9.21.27 and 9.20.30-S1, no workarounds, and no known active exploits.

claimChecks.claim: A high severity vulnerability in the most widely deployed DNS software just dropped
claimChecks.explanation: ISC rates CVE-2026-94300 High (CVSS 8.1) for BIND 9, but it was disclosed 21 Oct, needs GSS-TSIG plus a replayed signed message, and has no known active exploits.

incidents.name: Tailworm: 11 pre-patch Tailscale/headscale flaws disclosed; SSH root escalation fixed in v1.104.4
incidents.subject: Tailscale
incidents.summary: Cyberdione Labs publicly released its 'Tailworm' audit - 11 findings against Tailscale 1.104.2 and headscale 0.29.5, six rated high - over the Oct 24-25 weekend, before patches existed. Four findings concern Tailscale SSH and could turn a policy-authorized session into root on a target server via Unix-socket forwarding. Tailscale shipped v1.104.4 on Oct 28 fixing four bulletined issues and says exploitation needs an existing foothold, not unauthenticated access.
incidents.dateLabel: Disclosed publicly (pre-patch) Oct 24-25, 2026; Tailscale bulletins and investigation Oct 26-27; v1.104.4 shipped Oct 28

sources.label: Tailscale: Tailscale SSH - findings and fixes

incidents.correction: Despite the report's name, this is not self-replicating malware: every hop requires a device already authorized on the tailnet with SSH access permitted in policy. No in-the-wild exploitation has been reported by any party.

detail.whatHappened: Over the October 24-25 weekend, Cyberdione Labs publicly released 'Tailworm', an audit report listing 11 findings against Tailscale 1.104.2 and the self-hosted headscale 0.29.5 control server, all verified by reproduction in a lab - disclosed before any patch was available, a timing SecurityWeek reports drew criticism, while the researchers argued rapid awareness would speed remediation. Six findings are rated high severity and four concern Tailscale SSH, the SSH server built into the root-privileged tailscaled. The headline chain: Tailscale SSH performed Unix-socket forwarding operations as root, and the path allowlist meant to restrict them could be bypassed three ways (privileged dials via ssh -L, socket replacement via ssh -R unlinking root-owned sockets, and a path-check race), giving a policy-authorized peer with forwarding a route to root-only sockets such as the Docker socket or the tailscaled local API. In lab tests this produced root code execution on target servers and theft of enrollment keys usable to add rogue devices, and the researchers showed the chain could be automated to hop machine to machine in under a second per hop. Other findings cover app connectors (experimental conn25) translating traffic to attacker-chosen destinations without consulting network ACLs, unauthenticated memory exhaustion of the headscale control server, unbounded reads from a malicious DERP relay, and tailscale serve weaknesses.
detail.exposure: Exploitation of the SSH findings requires an existing foothold: a device already on the tailnet, Tailscale SSH access permitted in the policy file, and forwarding allowed by the access rules (granted automatically on headscale, per-rule on Tailscale's SaaS). Tailscale stresses the bugs do not let an unauthenticated attacker connect to arbitrary Tailscale SSH servers and does not recommend disabling Tailscale SSH outright. Self-hosted headscale servers face the unauthenticated control-server memory exhaustion from plain internet reachability. Everything was verified against Tailscale 1.104.2 and headscale 0.29.5. Because Tailscale SSH grants access by device identity rather than credentials, a chained attack needs no passwords or keys once one device is compromised.
detail.fix: Tailscale shipped v1.104.4 on October 28 fixing the four bulletined issues: TS-2026-014 (SSH Unix-socket forwarding now runs as the authenticated user instead of root), TS-2026-015 (SSH session memory is bounded and released on disconnect, preventing the tailscaled OOM crash that would kill every connection on the node), TS-2026-016 (serve TCP-to-Unix forwards are restricted and backend paths revalidated per connection) and TS-2026-017 (serve derives per-request capabilities instead of sharing them across HTTP/2 streams). Tailscale says it also added architectural safeguards against broader classes of related issues. Interim mitigation published during the investigation: set TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1 in the tailscaled service environment and restart, which disables forwarding without disabling Tailscale SSH, and review and tighten SSH access policies. Users are urged to upgrade to v1.104.4 or newer.
detail.remaining: Tailscale's bulletins and blog itemize the four fixed issues; they do not enumerate the status of all 11 Cyberdione findings - in particular the headscale-specific, app-connector (experimental) and DERP-client findings. headscale had no numbered patched release in the sources checked, and no CVEs are referenced in the vendor material. Whether any finding was exploited before disclosure is unknown; no party has reported in-the-wild use.

responses.summary: Called the issues serious, published four security bulletins and an investigation page, shipped v1.104.4 within days with fixes plus architectural safeguards, and published a findings-and-fixes post. It says the 'worm' framing is inaccurate: exploitation requires an authorized device with policy-permitted SSH access.
Published the 11-finding report publicly before patches existed, arguing rapid awareness would speed remediation, and updated the report as fixes landed in Tailscale's public repositories.
Reported the uncoordinated disclosure, Tailscale's rush to patch, and the wormable-chaining demonstration with the vendor's caveats.

claimChecks.claim: Tailworm is a worm that spreads automatically between machines
claimChecks.explanation: Researchers showed the SSH chain can be automated to hop in under a second per machine. Tailscale says that is not self-replicating malware: every hop requires policy-permitted SSH access from an already-authorized device.

claimChecks.claim: Anyone on the internet can exploit these flaws against a Tailscale node
claimChecks.explanation: The SSH findings require an authenticated, policy-authorized peer. The unauthenticated piece is the headscale control-server memory exhaustion, which affects self-hosted headscale, not Tailscale's hosted service.

incidents.name: Trojanized Claude Code 2.1.313 in Cursor's marketplace plants SSH backdoor
incidents.subject: Cursor
incidents.summary: A maliciously modified build of the Claude Code for VS Code extension, version 2.1.313, was served from Cursor's own extension marketplace for about eleven hours on Oct 29. Cursor says it was not developed by Anthropic and at most 5,000 users were affected. The build plants an attacker SSH key, tries to enable the SSH service, opens a persistent reverse tunnel and reports host details. The attacker server is offline; the planted key and persistence survive removing the extension.
incidents.dateLabel: Malicious build served Oct 29, 2026 ~2:27am-1:35pm PT; Cursor notice Oct 29; clean 2.1.314 published and X announcement Oct 30
incidents.correction: Early reports attributed the build to Open VSX (OpenSourceMalware initially, Phorion's advisory still says so); OpenSourceMalware corrected this after Cursor contacted it. Open VSX, npm and the Microsoft VS Code Marketplace never listed a 2.1.313 at all, and Anthropic's changelog skips from 2.1.312 to 2.1.314.

detail.whatHappened: Between about 2:27am and 1:35pm PT on October 29, 2026, Cursor's own VS Code extension marketplace served a maliciously modified build of the Claude Code for VS Code extension identifying itself as Anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.313. Cursor says the build was not developed by Anthropic and that an audit found no other tampered extensions. The malware is 66 lines prepended to extension.js, so it runs as soon as the extension loads - no Claude conversation needed. It collects host details, appends an attacker Ed25519 key (comment 'svc-telemetry') to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, tries to enable the local SSH service, opens a reverse SSH tunnel to tunnel@134.209.82.225 that forwards the machine's SSH port, installs persistence (macOS LaunchAgent com.apple.sysmond, Windows 'SysMon' scheduled task with a Startup-folder fallback, and per OpenSourceMalware a Linux @reboot cron entry), retries roughly every 60 seconds, and posts a host report over plain HTTP to 134.209.82.225:8099/beacon. Cursor removed the package, took the whole marketplace down, rotated its keys, rebuilt and restored it, published indicators and remediation scripts, and announced the incident on X on October 30. It says it worked with the hosting provider (ARIN places the IP in a DigitalOcean range) to take the attacker server offline. How the package entered the marketplace has not been explained, and no one has named who is behind it.
detail.exposure: Cursor says at most 5,000 users were affected: anyone who installed or updated Claude Code for VS Code from the Cursor marketplace during the window (darwin-arm64 and win32-x64 builds named). The SSH-enable step usually failed: it needs administrator rights the extension does not have on most macOS and Windows machines, and Phorion reports a likely bug in the macOS check for standard users. But the authorized_keys entry, the persistence files and the host report can all have landed anyway, and they survive updating or removing the extension. The implant collected hostname, username, OS and architecture, home and working directories, the global git email, the public IP, and the names (not values) of up to 40 environment variables containing KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASS, AWS or GCP - a map of which credentials a later interactive session through the tunnel could go after. The npm CLI package, the Open VSX extension and the Microsoft Marketplace extension were never affected; none of them has a 2.1.313.
detail.fix: Cursor asks all users to update Claude Code for VS Code to 2.1.314 or later, and anyone possibly in the window to run its published checks: search ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (and on Windows C:\ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys) for the 'svc-telemetry' key, matching the fingerprint SHA256:0Z6R+DF64Do2nwQic8a7kkfDLNNk4IiK+2U2Rci4htk rather than the comment alone; look for the persistence files (~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist, ~/.config/.smt and .smtk, the Windows SysMon task and sysmon.cmd Startup script); and look for long-running ssh or autossh processes with -R *:0:localhost:22 or connections to 134.209.82.225 on ports 22 or 8099. Cursor publishes remediation scripts for macOS (run as the affected user) and Windows (run as Administrator). If indicators are present: isolate the machine, remove the key, persistence and tunnel processes, rotate every credential the account could reach from a known-clean machine, and assess a rebuild - OpenSourceMalware advises rebuilding over assuming the known files were the whole compromise. Removing the extension alone does not remove the backdoor.
detail.remaining: The entry point into Cursor's marketplace is unexplained ('some form of compromise' is all Cursor told OpenSourceMalware), the operator is unnamed, and what was done through any tunnel that did connect is unknown. Anthropic has not published a statement that Rescana could find. No CVE has been assigned and none may be: this is a malicious build in one marketplace, not a flaw in Claude Code itself. OpenSourceMalware notes its analysis proves the specific artifact was malicious, not by itself how distribution happened.

responses.summary: Identified and removed the package, took down, key-rotated and rebuilt its marketplace, says at most 5,000 users were affected and that it will contact them directly, worked with the hosting provider to take 134.209.82.225 offline, and published indicators plus macOS and Windows remediation scripts.

Published the full technical analysis (with indicators and hashes), corrected its initial Open VSX attribution after Cursor reached out, and recommends treating loaded hosts as compromised with rebuild preferred over artifact removal.
Published an advisory with indicators; its Open VSX attribution is superseded by Cursor's notice. Notes the macOS SSH-enable step likely fails for standard users due to a bug in the malicious code.

claimChecks.claim: The official Claude Code extension was compromised on npm, Open VSX or the Microsoft marketplace
claimChecks.explanation: Cursor says the malicious 2.1.313 existed only in its own marketplace. Open VSX, npm and the Microsoft VS Code Marketplace have no 2.1.313 version at all, and OpenSourceMalware's updated post says those artifacts are not malicious.

claimChecks.claim: Updating or removing the extension removes the backdoor
claimChecks.explanation: The planted SSH key, persistence entries and host report survive extension updates and removal. Cursor advises running its checks and remediation whether or not the tunnel ever worked.

claimChecks.claim: The tunnel gave the attacker access on affected machines
claimChecks.explanation: Enabling the SSH service needs administrator rights the extension usually lacks, and Cursor says that step would fail outside highly unusual circumstances. The planted key, persistence and reconnaissance beacon can still have landed on those machines.

incidents.name: So-net/Plala: 2.58M subscriber records stolen from Sony's Japanese ISP, incl. 54k email passwords
incidents.subject: So-net (Sony Network Communications)
incidents.summary: Sony Network Communications says attackers were in the So-net member database from Oct 19 until detection on Oct 23. Roughly 2.58 million current and former So-net and Plala subscriber records were taken, plus about 54,000 email addresses with their passwords from four mail services, and 16 bank account records. Forced password resets began Oct 27. How they got in is undisclosed.
incidents.dateLabel: Intrusion Oct 19, detected Oct 23; disclosed Oct 27, 2026 with forced password resets the same day

sources.label: NTT Docomo notice for Plala S Course customers (Japanese)

incidents.correction: The 2.58M figure counts exposed subscriber records; the email-password leak is a smaller subset of about 54,000 accounts from four specific mail services, not every subscriber. So-net says it does not store credit card data.

detail.whatHappened: Attackers broke into the So-net member database on October 19, 2026. Sony Network Communications first spotted the intrusion on October 23, took the targeted server offline and cut traffic from the attackers, and by the next day had confirmed personal data was taken. It announced the breach on October 27. Of the roughly 2.6 million exposed records, 2.14 million belong to So-net subscribers and 443,000 to Plala (S Course) subscribers; about 293,000 relate to people who left the services in March 2026 or later, whose details are retained for final billing and support. The attackers also obtained approximately 54,000 email addresses together with their passwords from four mail services (Mail Service (G), A-Box, So-net VAIO Mail and PostPet mail), and 16 records containing bank account details (bank, branch, account type, account number, holder name - not PINs).
detail.exposure: Stolen subscriber data includes names, dates of birth, gender, phone numbers, email addresses, user IDs and the IDs customers use to connect to the internet. The email-password leak is the sharpest piece: So-net's FAQ says a third party holding those credentials was in a position to read, send and receive mail through email software and So-net Webmail until the resets. Credit card data is not involved because So-net does not store it, and the NURO service and other offerings do not appear affected.
detail.fix: The company took the targeted server offline and blocked the attackers' traffic on October 23, began forcing password resets for the impacted email accounts on October 27 (users must set a new password before resuming service), and reported the incident to Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission. NTT Docomo posted its own notice for affected Plala (S Course) customers.
detail.remaining: How the attackers got in has not been disclosed; the company lists the cause only as unauthorized access by a third party and says the investigation continues. Whether the stolen data has been misused or published is not addressed in the notices.

responses.summary: Disclosed the breach October 27 with per-service counts, an FAQ, and forced password resets for the ~54,000 leaked email accounts; reported to the Personal Information Protection Commission.
Posted a parallel apology and notice for Plala (S Course) customers whose information flowed out via the So-net systems.

claimChecks.claim: 2.6 million So-net customers had their passwords stolen
claimChecks.explanation: The 2.58M figure is subscriber records (names, contact details, IDs). Email passwords leaked for about 54,000 accounts across four named mail services; So-net says no password leaked for the free basic mailbox.

incidents.name: DHS: 40k+ employee records stolen and published, incl. CBP, ICE and CISA staff
incidents.subject: U.S. Department of Homeland Security
incidents.summary: A hacker using the handle 'Department of Peace' stole and published personnel records for more than 40,000 DHS employees - about a fifth of the department - including names, job titles, work contact details and which internal systems each person can access. TechCrunch verified part of the dataset as authentic; DHS says it is aware of a potential breach; Okta says it has no evidence its systems were compromised.
incidents.dateLabel: Records appear exfiltrated around mid-Aug 2026 per timestamps; published and reported Oct 28, 2026
incidents.correction: The hacker claims the data came from a DHS Okta single sign-on system. That vector is a claim, not established fact: Okta says it is secure and has no evidence its data or systems were compromised, and DHS has not confirmed any entry point.

detail.whatHappened: TechCrunch reported on October 28, 2026 that a hacker going by 'Department of Peace' stole reams of personnel data in a previously undisclosed breach at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and published it online. The dataset covers more than 40,000 employees: about 21,000 at Customs and Border Protection, 10,000 at Immigration and Customs Enforcement and its Homeland Security Investigations unit, just under 1,000 at CISA, and thousands more at headquarters, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. Record timestamps suggest exfiltration around mid-August. The data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew and shared with DDoSecrets, which hosts leaked datasets. TechCrunch verified a portion as authentic by matching named employees against an offline copy. The same hacker earlier this year claimed a separate theft of thousands of DHS contracts with private-sector vendors.
detail.exposure: The records include names, job titles, work email addresses, cell phone numbers and office locations, plus IT and login records showing which systems and internal apps each employee may access. Wired reports the leak includes undercover ICE agents. Beyond identities, the Active Directory group memberships map parts of the department's tooling: Microsoft 365, a 'Headspace_users' group of about 4,500 including ICE deportation officers (Headspace says its ICE contract ended in 2023), Penlink web-surveillance groups of up to 2,000+ across ICE's HSI unit, a 200+ user CBP group tied to the Mobile Fortify facial-recognition app, ChatGPT access groups including senior officials, and groups referencing investigations into Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.
detail.fix: A DHS spokesperson told TechCrunch after publication that the department 'is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation,' saying it takes threats against employees seriously and will update the public. No technical remediation or containment detail has been published. Okta said it was aware of the report, that 'Okta is secure,' and that it has no evidence its data or systems were compromised.
detail.remaining: How the breach was carried out is unknown - the hacker did not respond to TechCrunch's questions, the Okta-vector claim is unverified and disputed by Okta, and it is unclear whether the vulnerability has been fixed or when DHS became aware. The full dataset is larger than the verified sample, so the authentic portion establishes the leak is real without confirming every record in it.

responses.summary: Said DHS is aware of a potential breach, is working to address it, takes all security threats against employees and officers seriously, and will update the public when more information is available.
Said Okta is aware of the report, that Okta is secure, and that it has no evidence its data or systems were compromised.
Received the dataset via maia arson crimew and hosts it; co-founder Emma Best called it a catalyst for investigations and public-records requests.

claimChecks.claim: Okta was breached
claimChecks.explanation: The hacker claims the data came from DHS's Okta single sign-on system. Okta says it is secure with no evidence of compromise, and DHS has not confirmed any vector. The data may have been taken from a DHS-side system that Okta fronts.

incidents.name: Amadeus booking-system breach cascades across airlines: Korean Air, Asiana, JAL, ANA, Star Flyer confirm passenger data exposure
incidents.subject: Amadeus
incidents.summary: A vulnerability in Amadeus's travel booking display environment - disclosed Oct 1 as unexploited - turns out to have been abused: Korean Air and Asiana confirmed customer leaks Oct 23, JAL says unauthorized access ran from Aug 2023 to Sep 2026 and exposed ~92,000 customers' booking data (passport numbers for ~2,000), and ANA and Star Flyer posted their own notices. Amadeus serves 400+ airlines; the full scope is unconfirmed.
incidents.dateLabel: Amadeus disclosed the vulnerability Oct 1, 2026 (then said unexploited); Korean Air + Asiana confirmed leaks Oct 23; JAL notified Oct 23, disclosed Oct 28; ANA + Star Flyer notices Oct 29-30; JAL says access ran Aug 10, 2023 - Sep 23, 2026

sources.label: Star Flyer official notice (English) · Original source
Seoul Economic Daily · Korean Air + Asiana confirmation

incidents.correction: Amadeus's Oct 1 statement said the vulnerability had not been exploited by ransomware actors; subsequent airline confirmations show the flaw was maliciously exploited. JAL's ~90,000 + ~2,000 figures are JAL's customers only, not a total. Cathay Pacific posted a third-party incident notice, but its link to Amadeus is unconfirmed in the sources checked.

detail.whatHappened: Amadeus, whose Passenger Service System handles reservations, ticketing and check-in for more than 400 airlines, published a statement on October 1, 2026 saying it had found a vulnerability in its travel booking display environment that could expose traveler data - and at that time said ransomware actors had not exploited it and no payment data was involved. On October 23, Korean Air and Asiana confirmed customer information had leaked through the booking-system operator. JAL says Amadeus notified it the same day that unauthorized access to the system occurred between August 10, 2023 and September 23, 2026; JAL disclosed on October 28 that reservation codes (PNRs), names, flight dates, routes and travel classes for about 90,000 customers were exposed, with roughly 2,000 more customers also losing email addresses, phone numbers, passport numbers, nationalities, frequent-flyer numbers and ticket/seat numbers. ANA and Star Flyer posted their own breach notices on October 29-30, and Cathay Pacific posted a third-party security notice whose connection is unconfirmed.
detail.exposure: Per JAL: booking data (PNRs, names, dates, routes, classes) for ~90,000 customers, plus contact details, passport numbers and loyalty identifiers for ~2,000. JAL says credit card numbers and passwords were not compromised and that it has no evidence of misuse so far. The exposed PNR data is enough to view or social-engineer bookings, and the three-year access window means the airline-confirmed counts are likely a floor, not a ceiling: Amadeus also serves 210 airport operators, 34 cruise and ferry lines and 2 million hotels, and has not given a total.
detail.fix: Amadeus says it has implemented the necessary security measures, and JAL says flight operations are unaffected. Each affected airline is notifying its own customers under local rules. (ANA separately suspended some web and app services from October 21, but that action appears tied to the PHP2Shell threat, not this incident.)
detail.remaining: The total number of affected airlines and passengers is unconfirmed - BleepingComputer asked Amadeus whether more airlines and markets were hit and got no answer. Whether exploitation really began in August 2023 or earlier is unverified, and Amadeus has not explained the gap between its Oct 1 'not exploited' statement and the airline confirmations three weeks later.

responses.summary: Disclosed the Amadeus-sourced breach with per-category counts (~90k booking records, ~2k with passport and contact data), stated card data and passwords were not involved, and said operations are unaffected.
Posted their own notices confirming customer impact from unauthorized access to the Amadeus-provided Passenger Service System.

responses.by: Korean Air / Asiana (via Seoul Economic Daily)
responses.summary: First carriers to confirm customer data leaked through the booking-system operator, on October 23.

Published a vulnerability statement October 1 saying the flaw could expose traveler data but had not been exploited by ransomware actors; has not answered questions on total scope since airline confirmations began.

claimChecks.claim: Amadeus said on Oct 1 that the flaw was not exploited
claimChecks.verdict: accurate at the time, since superseded
claimChecks.explanation: The Oct 1 statement said ransomware actors had not exploited it. Korean Air, Asiana, JAL, ANA and Star Flyer have since confirmed malicious exploitation, with JAL citing an access window back to August 2023.

incidents.name: Warp: vendor exploit exposes AI agent traces and telemetry for roughly 1% of users
incidents.subject: Warp
incidents.summary: Warp's CEO says attackers ran an 'active and narrow-banded exploitation' of a third-party vendor in Warp's infrastructure, reaching agent decision traces and user telemetry for roughly 1% of users. The company detected it within hours, engaged CrowdStrike and law enforcement, and notified affected users. Whether source code, prompts or credentials were in the exposed data is undisclosed; analysis attributes the attack to an agent swarm.
incidents.dateLabel: Active exploitation detected and contained Oct 23, 2026 (within hours); CEO statement Oct 26; reported Oct 27

sources.label: Zach Lloyd (Warp CEO) statement · Original source

incidents.correction: The roughly 1% figure is the CEO's estimate of impacted users, not a confirmed count. 'Agent swarm' attribution comes from analysis of the incident, not from a named threat actor.

detail.whatHappened: On Friday, October 23, 2026, Warp became aware of what CEO Zach Lloyd describes as an active, narrow-banded exploitation of a vendor in Warp's infrastructure. The company says it detected the operation within hours and remediated. Agent traces - the decision logs of Warp's AI coding agents - and user telemetry were identified as potentially affected. Lloyd estimates roughly 1% of Warp's users (the platform claims at least 800,000) may have been impacted, and says affected users have been notified. Analysis of the incident suggests the attack was powered by an agent swarm using what Lloyd called a very sophisticated penetration and escalation technique.
detail.exposure: Identified as potentially affected: agent decision traces and telemetry. The company has not clarified whether the exposed data included source code, prompts, credentials or other sensitive content - agent traces for a coding tool can contain all three, so the practical exposure is wider than 'telemetry' suggests until Warp says otherwise.
detail.fix: Warp says it remediated and mitigated within hours of detection, contacted the vendor about the vulnerability, engaged CrowdStrike for the investigation, informed law enforcement, and notified impacted users. Users are advised to monitor account activity and treat unsolicited communications cautiously.
detail.remaining: The vendor is unnamed, the vulnerability undescribed, and the data categories actually taken (vs potentially affected) are not published. No group has claimed the attack. This lands one week after the OpenCode breach (stored API keys, unauthorized charges), making it the second AI coding platform hit in October.

responses.summary: Disclosed the vendor exploitation publicly, gave the ~1% impact estimate, described hours-level detection and remediation, and said CrowdStrike and law enforcement are engaged.

incidents.name: Cathedral says its AI agents got inside Anthropic in under 12 hours; Anthropic disputes the scope
incidents.subject: Anthropic
incidents.summary: Cathedral, a startup founded by former DOGE staffers, told the Washington Post its AI agents entered Anthropic internal systems via weaknesses in third-party business software, reaching meeting transcripts, salary and offer data, and Slack discussions about its most advanced models. Anthropic, which received the findings through its bug bounty program, says only a limited set of sales, HR and IT systems was reached, Claude conversations, source code and model weights were not affected, and Cathedral broke bounty rules by withholding activity.
incidents.dateLabel: Reported Oct 26, 2026 (Washington Post, draft Cathedral report); Anthropic cut access the same day it received the findings
incidents.correction: The headline claim is Cathedral's, from a draft report the Washington Post reviewed; Anthropic confirms an intrusion path existed but disputes how far it went, and says the startup violated bug-bounty rules by not disclosing everything it did. Neither side has published the report itself.

detail.whatHappened: Cathedral, a cybersecurity startup founded by former DOGE staffers, ran AI agents against Anthropic and says they found a way into internal systems in less than 12 hours by abusing weaknesses in third-party business software. Its draft report, reviewed by the Washington Post, claims access to meeting transcripts, salary and job-offer data, and Slack discussions about Anthropic's most advanced models. The findings reached Anthropic through its bug bounty program. Anthropic says only a limited set of sales, HR and IT systems was reached, that it cut off the startup's access the same day, and that Claude conversations, source code and model weights were not affected. It also accuses Cathedral of breaking the bounty program's rules by not disclosing all of its activity.
detail.exposure: Disputed. Cathedral's claimed reach: meeting transcripts, compensation data, and model-related Slack discussions. Anthropic's confirmed reach: a limited set of sales, HR and IT systems; explicitly not Claude conversations, source code or model weights. The truth matters beyond Anthropic: the entry path was third-party business software, the same class of weakness behind this month's Warp and OpenCode incidents.
detail.fix: Anthropic says it cut off the startup's access the same day it received the findings. No customer action is indicated by either side.
detail.remaining: The draft report is unpublished, so Cathedral's claims are unverified beyond what Anthropic confirms. Whether Cathedral's activity stayed within bug-bounty scope is contested. The episode undercuts both easy narratives: autonomous agents reached a leading AI lab's business systems in hours, and the loudest version of the claim comes from the people selling the capability.

responses.summary: Confirmed receiving the findings via bug bounty, says reach was limited to sales, HR and IT systems, denies impact to Claude conversations, source code and model weights, cut access same-day, and accuses Cathedral of violating bounty rules by withholding activity.
Claims its AI agents reached meeting transcripts, salary and offer data, and Slack discussions about advanced models within 12 hours by abusing third-party business software weaknesses.

claimChecks.claim: AI agents hacked Anthropic in under 12 hours
claimChecks.explanation: Anthropic confirms an intrusion path into some business systems existed and was closed the same day. The claimed depth (transcripts, salaries, model Slack) is Cathedral's and disputed by Anthropic; core systems (conversations, code, weights) were not affected per Anthropic.

incidents.name: CVE-2026-97631: 16-year-old pre-boot RCE in TianoCore EDK II threatens most servers via PXE boot
incidents.subject: TianoCore EDK II (UEFI firmware)
incidents.summary: A buffer overflow in the PXE boot driver of TianoCore EDK II - the open-source UEFI code underneath most server firmware from AMI, Insyde and Phoenix - lets an attacker on the local network hang the boot or, with knowledge of the firmware build, execute code at the highest privilege before Secure Boot applies. Found by Anthropic and Google researchers, it went public months early after AMI published a fix, breaking the planned January disclosure embargo.
incidents.dateLabel: Fix PR public Oct 14, 2026 (embargo broken; planned disclosure was January); Ars Technica Oct 27, oss-security Oct 28

sources.label: oss-security: CVE-2026-97631 pre-boot RCE in EDK II PXE driver

incidents.correction: Only machines that boot over the network (PXE) are exposed, and code execution needs knowledge of the target's firmware build; an attacker otherwise gets a boot hang. This is not remote-from-the-internet: it needs local network access during boot.

detail.whatHappened: A 16-year-old buffer overflow (CVE-2026-97631) sits in the NetworkPkg UefiPxeBcDxe driver of TianoCore EDK II, the open-source UEFI implementation that most server vendors ship through firmware suppliers such as AMI, Insyde and Phoenix. An attacker with local network access can send an oversized ICMP error message to a machine while it boots over the network (PXE), hanging the boot process or - if the target's firmware build is known - running code at the highest privilege level, before Secure Boot and the OS's defenses exist. The flaw was found by Anthropic and Google researchers. It became public months ahead of a planned January disclosure when AMI published a code fix, forcing organizations to chase firmware updates from their individual vendors.
detail.exposure: Most servers worldwide carry EDK II-derived firmware, but the exploitable surface is narrower: only machines configured for network boot, and only from the local network during the boot window. Data centers using PXE provisioning at scale are the real risk population.
detail.fix: The upstream fix is tianocore/edk2 PR #13302 (public since Oct 14). Because EDK II reaches machines through firmware suppliers, remediation means firmware updates from each server vendor; there is no OS-level patch. Where firmware updates are pending, disabling unused PXE boot removes the exposure.
detail.remaining: Which vendors have shipped patched firmware, and for which models, is untracked centrally. Whether the broken embargo leaves a usable exploit window is unquantified - no in-the-wild exploitation has been reported.

responses.summary: Fix merged upstream as PR #13302; AMI's early publication of its code fix broke the coordinated January embargo and made the flaw public.

claimChecks.claim: The flaw threatens most servers on the planet
claimChecks.explanation: EDK II-derived firmware ships in most servers, but exploitation requires local network access and PXE network boot, and reliable code execution needs the target's firmware build. The at-risk set is PXE-booted machines, not every server.

incidents.name: Cloudflare Workers AI cross-tenant leak: 155 GLM-5.3 responses carried other customers' data
incidents.subject: Cloudflare
incidents.summary: A configuration mismatch (KV cache smaller than the advertised context window) plus an SGLang bug let over-length requests to GLM-5.3 on Workers AI read cache data left by other customers' sessions. Cloudflare says 155 responses between Aug 27 and Sep 9 were affected, all with prompts over 681,280 tokens; it found no evidence of deliberate exploitation, fixed the issue after a HackerOne report, and SGLang shipped the fix in 0.5.22.
incidents.dateLabel: Leak window Aug 27 - Sep 9, 2026; reported via HackerOne (Knostic's Gadi Evron); Cloudflare disclosure and fix Oct 26; SGLang fix in 0.5.22
incidents.correction: 155 affected responses over a two-week window, all tied to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens on one model - not a general Workers AI leak. Cloudflare reports no evidence of deliberate exploitation.

detail.whatHappened: Between August 27 and September 9, 2026, 155 responses from the GLM-5.3 model on Cloudflare's Workers AI platform contained data from other customers' recent requests to the same model. The cause was a configuration mismatch that left the model's KV cache smaller than its advertised context window, combined with a bug in the SGLang inference engine that allowed over-length requests (longer than 681,280 tokens) to read cache data left behind by earlier sessions. Knostic researcher Gadi Evron reported the issue through HackerOne; Cloudflare fixed it and disclosed on October 26.
detail.exposure: Fragments of other tenants' prompts and context returned inside model responses - a cross-tenant data leak inside a hosted AI inference service. Cloudflare counts 155 affected responses, all on GLM-5.3 and all involving very long prompts, and says it found no evidence anyone exploited the condition deliberately.
detail.fix: Cloudflare corrected the configuration and patched its deployment; the upstream SGLang fix shipped in version 0.5.22, and Cloudflare recommends SGLang operators update. The disclosure credits the HackerOne report and coordinates with SGLang.
detail.remaining: What data actually appeared in the 155 responses is not enumerated, and affected customers' notification status is not described in the public posts. Other hosted SGLang deployments may have the same bug until they update.

responses.summary: Published a full root-cause and remediation post: configuration mismatch plus SGLang bug, 155 affected responses, no evidence of deliberate exploitation, fix deployed, coordinated with SGLang on the 0.5.22 upstream fix.
Reported the cross-tenant exposure via HackerOne and published a research write-up on the KV-cache reuse condition.

incidents.name: University of Copenhagen breach: data of ~525,000 people, incl. national ID numbers and 20k card PINs
incidents.subject: University of Copenhagen
incidents.summary: Hackers reached one of the university's test environments and took personal data on about 525,000 current and former members - names, phone numbers, personal emails, and CPR national identity numbers for many - plus the PIN codes for roughly 20,000 staff and student ID cards, since reissued. Detected and contained Oct 20; attacker and motive unknown.
incidents.dateLabel: Attack detected and contained Oct 20, 2026; disclosed Oct 23; card PINs reissued after disclosure

sources.label: University of Copenhagen news · Original source

incidents.correction: The 525,000 figure covers current and former members of the university community whose data sat in the compromised test environment; CPR numbers were included for many, not all, and the 20,000 PINs are for university ID cards, not payment cards.

detail.whatHappened: The University of Copenhagen says attackers gained access to one of its test environments and obtained personal data on about 525,000 current and former members of the university community. The attack was detected on October 20, 2026 and contained. The university disclosed the breach on October 23.
detail.exposure: Names, phone numbers and personal email addresses, along with Danish national identity (CPR) numbers for many of those affected - CPR numbers are the sensitive core, since they enable identity fraud. The PIN codes for the ID cards of roughly 20,000 staff and students were also compromised and have been reissued.
detail.fix: The university contained the incident on detection, reissued the compromised card PINs, and published a breach notification page with guidance for affected people.
detail.remaining: The university says it does not know who is behind the attack or the motive. Why a test environment held live personal data at this scale, and whether the data has been used or published, is unaddressed publicly.

responses.summary: Disclosed the breach with counts and data categories, confirmed containment, reissued ~20,000 ID-card PINs, and published a notification page for affected people.

incidents.name: FEC takes campaign-finance filing system offline after attempted breach, a week before US midterms
incidents.subject: US Federal Election Commission
incidents.summary: The FEC shut down parts of its electronic filing system after cybersecurity staff noticed attempted intrusions, a person familiar with the situation told POLITICO - in the final week before the November 3 midterms, blocking the 24/48-hour campaign-finance reports. Past filings stayed searchable and the FEC initially declined to explain the outage. The system was restored Oct 28. An attempted intrusion and an availability hit; no data theft is confirmed.
incidents.dateLabel: Attempted breach and shutdown reported Oct 27, 2026; system restored Oct 28; midterms Nov 3
incidents.correction: Reported as attempted intrusions, not a confirmed compromise: the FEC shut the attacked components down to contain them, and no data theft or alteration has been established in the sources cited.

detail.whatHappened: The Federal Election Commission's electronic filing system went offline in the final week before the November 3, 2026 midterm elections. POLITICO reports, from a person familiar with the situation granted anonymity to discuss an ongoing internal investigation, that FEC cybersecurity staff 'noticed attempted intrusions and were able to shut down' the parts of the filing system being attacked, describing the incident as 'quite narrow and compartmentalized.' The Washington Post had earlier reported the system down with the agency declining to say why. The outage blocked the 24-hour and 48-hour reports that track last-minute campaign spending on specific races, while past filings remained searchable. Some systems remained down through Tuesday evening, October 27; the system was restored on October 28.
detail.exposure: Availability, not (so far) data: campaigns and political groups could not file required last-minute spending disclosures during the outage. No theft or modification of filings has been reported. The FEC does not administer elections or count ballots, so voting itself is unaffected.
detail.fix: FEC cybersecurity staff shut down the attacked parts of the filing system to contain the attempt, and service was restored on October 28. The agency initially declined public comment on the cause.
detail.remaining: Who attempted the intrusion, what they reached before the shutdown, and why the agency would not initially explain the outage are unanswered in the reporting. Whether any filing deadlines were formally extended is unconfirmed.

responses.summary: Cybersecurity staff noticed the attempted intrusions early, shut down the attacked components ('quite narrow and compartmentalized'), and restored the system October 28; the agency had declined to explain the outage when first asked.

incidents.name: Northflank breach: customer environment variables decrypted, stored AI API keys abused
incidents.subject: Northflank
incidents.summary: Northflank, a cloud deployment platform, told all customers on Oct 30 to assume their environment variables have been decrypted and to rotate every secret immediately. Users report unauthorised use of AI API keys stored on the platform, and Northflank links the activity to the 'Black October' wave of attacks on AI developer platforms tracked by Wiz. Parts of the platform are in major outage while it patches.
incidents.dateLabel: Wiz threat alert and first Northflank patches Oct 30, 2026 ~11:43-13:05 UTC; MySQL/Redis secret rotation opened to all customers Oct 31 13:34 UTC; rotation guidance and partial outage ongoing

sources.label: Wiz · 'Black October' for AI Developer Platforms

detail.whatHappened: On October 30, 2026 at 11:43 UTC Northflank received a threat alert from Wiz and began patching its network policies within the hour, with Wiz's incident response team engaged by 13:00 UTC. At 13:58 UTC Northflank told all users to assume every environment variable stored on the platform had been decrypted and to rotate all keys immediately. By evening it reported that multiple users were confirming unauthorised use of AI API keys they had supplied to the platform, and on October 30 at 23:38 UTC it said the reports 'may be consistent with the broader pattern of attacks targeting AI credentials', pointing at the attacker IP addresses in Wiz's 'Black October' report. Large parts of the platform (networking, certificates, services, addons, jobs, builds, logs and metrics) are in major outage while the investigation continues; the app and API stay up. Northflank has not yet explained the initial access path.
detail.exposure: Potentially every secret stored on Northflank: workload environment variables, secret groups and global secrets - for all customers, including free-tier users. The confirmed harm so far is unauthorised use of stored AI provider keys; Northflank asks users to review their AI provider usage and billing logs. Wiz reports that across this month's campaign, stolen keys are validated within minutes and then used for LLMjacking at scale, and that around $371,000 in cryptocurrency was allegedly taken using keys stored at another breached platform.
detail.fix: Northflank's guidance: revoke and replace every secret stored on the platform with the issuing provider, update the affected secrets and workloads in Northflank, and disable public access on addons where enabled. It has force-enabled secret rotation on Postgres and MongoDB addons, opened secret rotation for MySQL and Redis to all customers (Oct 31 13:34 UTC), enabled audit logs for all customers including free users, and asks anyone seeing suspicious AI key usage to report it to Northflank support and the provider.
detail.remaining: The entry point and full scope are unconfirmed; Northflank says only that its investigation is ongoing. Whether the attackers are the same 'agent swarm' behind this month's other AI platform breaches is not established. How many customers' keys were actually abused, and what else the decrypted secrets opened up (databases, addons, downstream SaaS), is unknown. A post-incident report has not been published.

responses.summary: Acknowledged the incident the same day, ordered blanket secret rotation, force-enabled Postgres/MongoDB rotation, opened MySQL/Redis rotation to all customers (Oct 31 13:34 UTC) and enabled audit logs for all customers, and is publishing rolling updates while parts of the platform remain in major outage.

Its threat alert triggered Northflank's response. Its 'Black October' report counts Northflank as the ninth AI developer platform breached this month and describes the shared pattern: targeted theft of stored environment variables feeding LLMjacking and key resale.

claimChecks.claim: Northflank customer environment variables were decrypted
claimChecks.explanation: This is Northflank's own guidance: 'Assume all environment variables have been decrypted. Disable/rotate all keys.' Users have confirmed unauthorised use of stored AI keys.

claimChecks.claim: The Northflank breach is part of the coordinated October campaign against AI platforms
claimChecks.explanation: Wiz lists Northflank as the ninth incident in its 'Black October' campaign tracking and Northflank says attacker IPs overlap, but also notes the incidents are still being analysed and no single root cause links them.

incidents.name: Bunny CDN pulls Armenia node after infrastructure provider intrusion, reissues TLS certificates
incidents.subject: bunny.net
incidents.summary: One of bunny.net's infrastructure providers reported unauthorised access through third-party server management software, and a Bunny CDN node in Armenia sat on an affected server. Bunny cut it from rotation within 20 minutes, wiped it and says neither investigation found evidence the server was actually accessed - but it reissued all platform TLS certificates and is rotating managed customer certificates as a precaution.
incidents.dateLabel: Provider intrusion reported to bunny.net 'last week'; public notice Oct 29, 2026; managed certificate reissuance expected complete by end of Oct 31

detail.whatHappened: An infrastructure provider used by bunny.net reported unauthorised access involving third-party server management software. One Bunny CDN node, located in Armenia, was hosted on a server supplied by that provider. After the alert, bunny.net says its engineers stopped routing traffic through the server within 20 minutes, preserved logs, securely wiped the machine, revoked its access to other systems and permanently removed it from the CDN. Both bunny.net's investigation and the provider's found no evidence the server or its data was accessed, but bunny.net says it cannot completely rule that out. It disclosed the incident publicly on October 29, 2026. The provider is not named.
detail.exposure: If the server was accessed, the potentially exposed data would have been temporarily cached CDN content, Pull Zone configurations and TLS certificates stored on that one node. bunny.net says no account data was stored on the server and no internal systems were affected.
detail.fix: bunny.net revoked and reissued all TLS certificates for its platform domains (b-cdn.net and bunny.run) and is reissuing managed certificates for custom domains in controlled batches, expected to finish by end of October 31; existing certificates keep working until replaced and no action is needed from managed-certificate customers. Customers who manage their own TLS certificates are advised to revoke and reissue them with new private keys as a precaution.
detail.remaining: Whether the attacker ever reached the bunny.net server is unresolved - neither side found evidence of access, but bunny.net explicitly cannot rule it out. The infrastructure provider and the third-party management software are unnamed, and the provider's investigation is still running. It is not stated whether other bunny.net suppliers use the same software.

responses.summary: Contained the affected node within 20 minutes of the provider's alert, disclosed publicly with a plain-English account of what could and could not have been exposed, and is rotating all affected certificate material at its own cost rather than waiting for proof of access.

claimChecks.claim: Bunny CDN customer data was stolen
claimChecks.explanation: Neither bunny.net's nor the provider's investigation found evidence of access to the server. The certificate rotation is precautionary, and no account data was on the node.

claimChecks.claim: The incident was limited to one CDN node in Armenia
claimChecks.explanation: bunny.net says a single node hosted on the affected provider's server was involved, and that it was permanently removed from the infrastructure.

incidents.name: Akamai warns Linode customers over critical Linux kernel RCE CVE-2026-98432
incidents.subject: Linode (Akamai)
incidents.summary: Akamai opened a customer security advisory for Linode over CVE-2026-98432, a critical (CVSS 9.8) remote, unauthenticated use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 stack published Oct 15. It is deploying mitigations and telling customers to apply OS updates as they land. There is no evidence of exploitation on the platform - this is an advisory, not a confirmed breach.
incidents.dateLabel: CVE-2026-98432 published Oct 15, 2026; Red Hat critical advisory; Akamai/Linode customer advisory opened Oct 30, mitigation work ongoing Oct 31
incidents.correction: Reached the Hacker News front page as 'Linode Security Incident', but Akamai's advisory describes investigation and mitigation of a published kernel CVE - it explicitly reports no evidence of exploitation on the Akamai Compute platform. An advisory over a critical shared-infrastructure vulnerability, not a confirmed breach.

detail.whatHappened: CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 networking: tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers ownership of ireq->ireq_opt to the child socket without copying it, and a concurrent CPU processing a retransmitted SYN can then free the same memory. It is remotely exploitable by an unauthenticated attacker and rated CVSS 9.8 (critical); Red Hat issued a critical security bulletin and is expediting fixes. On October 30, 2026 Akamai opened a customer advisory for its Linode cloud platform, saying it was investigating impact, deploying mitigations for the known attack vector, and monitoring the platform in parallel.
detail.exposure: Any unpatched Linux host accepting IPv4 connections is potentially exposed to remote code execution; for Linode customers that means their own VMs until OS updates are applied. Akamai reports no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited on the Akamai Compute platform.
detail.fix: Apply OS kernel updates from the upstream distribution as soon as they become available. Akamai says it is deploying platform-level mitigations for the known attack vector while it analyses further impact, and points customers at its support tickets for questions.
detail.remaining: Akamai's investigation is still open: whether any Linode host was exposed before mitigations, and whether the vulnerability is being exploited anywhere in the wild, is unstated. Distribution kernel fixes were still rolling out when the advisory was published.

responses.summary: Opened a customer security advisory the day the issue reached it, committed to deploying mitigations for the known attack vector, and is posting progress updates while telling customers to patch their workloads.
Issued critical bulletin RHSB-2026-016 and is expediting kernel fixes across affected releases.

claimChecks.claim: Linode was breached
claimChecks.explanation: Akamai's advisory covers investigation and mitigation of a published kernel CVE and says it has no evidence of exploitation on the Akamai Compute platform.

claimChecks.claim: CVE-2026-98432 is remotely exploitable without authentication
claimChecks.explanation: NVD scores it CVSS 9.8 with network attack vector and no privileges required; Red Hat describes a remote, unauthenticated attacker being able to trigger the use-after-free.

incidents.name: Scribd confirms unauthorized access to systems; user emails and partial card metadata exposed
incidents.subject: Scribd (Everand, Slideshare, Fable)
incidents.summary: Scribd, Inc. is notifying users in phases that an unauthorized third party gained access to its systems and reached user information across Scribd, Slideshare, Everand and Fable. For most accounts this was basic account information; the notification email lists email address, last 4 digits of credit card with country, card issuer, card expiry date and payment history (not full card details). A smaller number of accounts had more sensitive information involved, not further specified. Scribd says it shut down the access and has no evidence of misuse.
incidents.dateLabel: Scribd help-center incident page stamped Oct 1, 2026; user notifications phased via Epiq, at least one received Oct 26, 2026; first wide public discussion Oct 31. Intrusion and discovery dates not stated

sources.label: Scribd Help Center · Information about the recent security incident

incidents.correction: Reached the Hacker News front page on Oct 31 as a fresh 'Tell HN: Scribd Breached', but Scribd's help-center page for the incident predates the thread (stamped October 1, 2026) and notices are being sent in phases - disclosure began earlier in October, and the actual incident date is unstated.

detail.whatHappened: An unauthorized third party gained access to one of Scribd, Inc.'s systems and used that access to reach other internal systems holding user information across Scribd, Slideshare, Everand and Fable. Scribd says it detected the activity, shut down the access, closed the vulnerability, engaged outside forensic and cybersecurity experts, and notified law enforcement and the relevant data protection authorities. Affected users are being notified in phases by Epiq, Scribd's notification partner; one recipient posted their notice (received Monday, October 26, 2026) to Hacker News on October 31, bringing the incident to wide attention.
detail.exposure: For most accounts, Scribd describes the data as basic account information. The notification email posted to Hacker News specifies: email address, last 4 digits of credit card and country, credit card issuer, card expiry date, and payment history (not including full credit card details). Scribd's help-center page adds that a smaller number of accounts had more sensitive information involved, without saying what. The number of affected users has not been disclosed, and Scribd reports no evidence the data has been misused.
detail.fix: Scribd recommends resetting your password on Scribd, Slideshare, Everand and Fable out of caution, and treating any message claiming to be from those brands that asks for a password or personal information as phishing - the company says it never asks for those by email, text or phone. Affected users are notified by Epiq on Scribd's behalf (check spam too), and a dedicated call center (+1-877-361-9887) handles incident questions.
detail.remaining: What the 'more sensitive information' for the smaller cohort was, how many users are affected, when the intrusion happened, when Scribd discovered it, and how the attacker got in are all unstated. The help-center page's October 1 update stamp versus the phased notifications (at least one received October 26) leaves the disclosure timeline unclear.

responses.summary: Published a help-center incident page, shut down the unauthorized access, closed the vulnerability, engaged outside forensic and cybersecurity experts, notified law enforcement and data protection authorities, and began phased user notifications via Epiq with a dedicated call center.

claimChecks.claim: Scribd suffered a breach of user data
claimChecks.explanation: Scribd's own help-center page confirms an unauthorized third party gained access to its systems, used it to reach other internal systems, and accessed user information; affected users are being notified via Epiq.

claimChecks.claim: Full credit card details were exposed
claimChecks.explanation: The notification email posted to Hacker News lists only the last 4 digits of the card, country, issuer, expiry date and payment history, and explicitly excludes full credit card details.

claimChecks.claim: The breach became public with the October 31 Hacker News thread
claimChecks.explanation: Scribd's help-center page on the incident is stamped October 1, 2026 and notifications are phased, so disclosure began earlier in October; the Oct 31 thread is the first wide public discussion, not a confirmed start of disclosure.
